newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam seeks place on world's newsstands.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam seeks place on world's newsstands.

text.p: Vietnam, showing apparent frustration at the shortcomings of its state-controlled media, said on Tuesday it had instructed magazines and journals to shape up and spread the word better, especially overseas.
Publications should be revamped, the English-language Vietnam News quoted government and other officials as telling a seminar for business editors last week in Ho Chi Minh City.
"In general, many stories are dull, lengthy, and just plain boring," said Tran Phu Son, head of Vietnam's Book and Magazine Import and Export Corporation.

The Vietnam News report quoted Son as saying there was growing demand abroad for news of the country's economic development, and said this was especially true among members of the roughly two million-strong community of overseas Vietnamese.
"With high duties and transport costs, we keep foreign readers from accessing comprehensive information about Vietnam," Son said.
Vietnam's media operates under tight state controls with editors-in-chief held legally responsible for ensuring that content is in line with prevailing Communist Party thinking.
Content is generally dominated by dry reports and grainy photos depicting a glowing picture of socialist economic achievements, with a noticeable absence of critical detail.

The number of publications has expanded rapidly in recent years and now stands at around 350. Despite this, and the availability of several of them in foreign languages, few have made significant inroads into overseas markets.

Consequently, the chief avenue of information about Vietnam to people outside the country has been foreign news organisations, which have been criticised by Hanoi for failing to understand its socialist system.
